phases.name: RUN — THREADING THE GAPS
phases.lead: Run the supply ships through the open gaps to the base, knowing each delivery teaches the enemy to close the gap you used.

routes.name: MOON SHADOW
routes.desc: The sensor blind spot behind the moon's bulk.
routes.tradeoff: The clearest gap, but the most obvious; the enemy closes it first once you use it.

routes.name: DEBRIS FIELD
routes.desc: The cluttered approach through floating wreckage.
routes.tradeoff: Hard for the enemy to watch, but hard for the supply ships to fly through without losing one.

protocol.Run clearance: The codeword SLACK WATER launches a run when a gap reads open.
protocol.Abort signal: The codeword EBB recalls the group if the gap closes mid-run, before the supply ships are too far in to turn back.

phases.name: RESOLUTION — THE LAST RUN
phases.lead: Keep the garrison supplied to the end, and decide whether the last delivery is worth a covered gap once the safe ones are gone.

sidebarKernel.kernel: whether enough has reached the base to outlast the siege, and whether the last run can be made safely or has to be forced.

assetDetails.detail: They are fragile and barely armed. Staying hidden and timing the run is their only defense, and a single one caught in the open is cargo the base needed, lost for good.
It holds only because the runs keep getting through. It will run out of supplies before you run out of safe gaps, and it cannot break the ground siege without the reinforcements the lander carries.

title: OPERATION THIN CORDON
skeleton: an interdiction force too small for the perimeter must impose a contraband blockade around a port region to choke a splinter garrison's arms resupply, reading which of many small civilian-screened runners is the real shipment among decoy fishing and freight traffic, where stopping everything strangles the population the contract forbids harming and stopping nothing lets the one shipment through that arms the holdouts
inspiration: the contraband-control blockade and the problem of neutral-flagged blockade runners, naval interdiction 1914-1918
situation: A small enemy garrison is holding a port city, and it can only hold because ships keep sneaking arms in by sea. When the front line broke on {WORLD}, a {TARGET_FACTION} loyalist remnant dug into the port district of {DISTRICT}. They refuse to surrender. As long as small boats keep bringing them ammunition and parts along the coast, they can keep fighting. {EMPLOYER} has hired your company to shut that supply line down. You will set up a blockade along the coast, stop and search boats, and cut off the garrison's supplies until it runs out of things to fight with. The problem is that the coast is far too long for your company to cover. It is crowded with fishing harbors, cargo docks, and shallow channels. Ordinary boats fill the water every day, from fishing trawlers to small barges to cargo ships. A few times a week, one of those boats is a smuggler carrying weapons. The smugglers hide in the everyday traffic. Weapons ride in a fishing boat, or parts ride under a fake cargo list. Sometimes they send an obvious boat as a decoy to pull your patrols away from the real cargo slipping through a channel you left open. If you stop and search every boat, you cut off a whole coast of people who have done nothing wrong. That is both a war crime and a gift to the enemy, who will use it to win support and recruits. If you stop too few boats, the one shipment that matters slips through. Your information about which boats carry weapons comes from informer tips and cargo-list checks. It is about a day old, and the smugglers feed you fake tips to throw you off. You have to pick the few smuggling boats out of a busy, working sea, and your company cannot watch all of it.

objectives.primary: Set up a blockade on the sea approaches to {DISTRICT}. Cut the garrison's seaborne weapon supply low enough that it can no longer keep fighting.
objectives.secondary: Stop and seize the smuggled cargo itself, meaning the ammunition, parts, and weapons. Do more than just scare the smugglers off.
objectives.bonus: Find and arrest the smuggling ring on shore that organizes the runs, so the supply line stays shut after your blockade ends.

complications.name: Too Much Coast, Too Few Hulls
complications.text: The coast is longer than your company can watch. Wherever you gather your patrols, you leave other channels open. The smugglers watch where your boats go and slip through the gaps. Every stretch of water you cover is a stretch you had to pull patrols away from somewhere else.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Your patrols are a limited resource stretched across the whole coast. If you cover one approach heavily, you leave others open. The smugglers send their cargo through whatever gaps your patrol pattern creates.

complications.name: The Boat That Matters Looks Like the Rest
complications.text: Each smuggler hides among the everyday boats. A weapons boat looks just like a fishing trawler. A parts run carries an honest-looking cargo list. A decoy boat is sent to pull your patrol away from the real cargo. Your only clues are a day-old tip and a cargo list that may be faked, so telling the boats apart is the hard part.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Smuggling boats are mixed in with civilian boats and decoys. If you send a patrol to search the wrong boat, you waste that patrol and let a real shipment pass somewhere else. Searching too many civilian boats also damages your reputation.

complications.name: Strangling the Wrong People
complications.text: If you stop and search every boat, the coast's people cannot work or eat. That means fishermen, freight crews, and the families who live on the water. The enemy wants exactly that. Hungry, angry people give them new recruits, public sympathy, and a propaganda win. So your blockade has to stop the smugglers without punishing the ordinary people around them.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Searching too many boats hurts ordinary people, and that pushes them toward the enemy and brings the enemy more recruits. A blockade that stops everything actually helps the enemy. It makes the rebellion worse instead of ending it.

decisionPoints.name: How to Run the Cordon
decisionPoints.context: You cannot search every boat, and you cannot let them all pass. How you set up the blockade decides which weakness the smugglers can use against you.

options.title: Tight cordon, search everything
advantages: Catches the most smuggled cargo because you miss the fewest boats
Shows clear control of the sea approaches
Leaves the smugglers little room to slip through
disadvantages: Shuts down the honest boats and starves the coast's people
Wins the enemy more support with every boat you hold up
Spreads your company so thin that no stretch of coast is well guarded
options.consequence: You catch more smuggled cargo, but the people come to hate you. That does the enemy's recruiting for them.

costs.resource: you lose the goodwill of the coast's people
costs.risk: the suffering of ordinary people boosts enemy support and the rebellion spreads

options.title: Selective interdiction on intelligence
advantages: Stops only the boats you suspect and leaves the honest boats alone
Keeps the coast working and the people on the fence
Puts your patrols where the smuggled cargo actually is
disadvantages: Only works if your tips are good, and your tips are poor and full of fakes
One wrong guess lets the real shipment slip past
The smugglers feed you false information to send your patrols the wrong way
options.consequence: You act only on your tips, and you accept that the tips will sometimes be wrong.

costs.resource: you have to rely on tips that are old and full of fakes
costs.risk: false information pulls your patrols away and the weapons shipment gets through untouched

options.title: Choke point, force the traffic
advantages: Puts your patrols on the few deep channels that big ships must use
Forces the smuggled cargo through water you can actually watch
Makes the best use of a company too small to cover the whole coast
disadvantages: Gives up the shallow channels to small smuggling boats
A fixed choke point is a pattern the smugglers can go around
Misses any cargo light enough to move through the shallows
options.consequence: You guard the main channels and give up the back channels. You are betting the heavy cargo needs deep water.

costs.resource: you give up the shallow approaches
costs.risk: the smugglers switch to small boats in the shallows and sneak the cargo through a little at a time

decisionPoints.name: A Suspected Runner in the Lane
decisionPoints.context: A boat your informers flagged is heading toward a shallow channel. It sits low in the water, and its cargo list claims a load of fish. Boarding it takes time and ties up a patrol. It could be the weapons shipment, a decoy, or just an honest fishing boat.

options.title: Board and search it
advantages: Proves right away whether the boat is clean or not
Seizes the weapons if the tip is good
Shows the blockade has real teeth
disadvantages: Boarding ties up a patrol while the rest of the channel goes unwatched
If it is a decoy, the real shipment slips through the gap you just made
If the boat is honest, another civilian crew turns against you
options.consequence: You commit to the boat in front of you. You find out whether the tip was the real shipment, a decoy, or just an innocent crew's bad luck.

costs.resource: one patrol tied up on a single boarding
costs.risk: the flagged boat is a decoy and the real cargo runs the channel you left open

options.title: Shadow it to its landing
advantages: Following the boat may reveal the smuggling ring on shore that receives it
Catches both the weapons and the people organizing the runs
Turns one stop into rolling up the whole supply line
disadvantages: A smuggler who spots the tail dumps the cargo or runs
Ties up the patrol for the whole trip, not just a quick boarding
You may lose both the weapons and the lead and get nothing
options.consequence: You let the boat run so you can see where it lands. You are betting it leads you to the smuggling ring before it slips away.

costs.resource: you hold off the seizure to follow the boat
costs.risk: the smuggler spots the tail, dumps the weapons, and you lose both the shipment and the lead

options.title: Wave it on, watch the lane
advantages: Keeps the patrol free to cover the whole approach
Avoids tying up force on an unconfirmed hull
Spares an honest crew if the tip is wrong
disadvantages: If it was the shipment, the weapons reach the enemy garrison
Letting a flagged boat pass looks like the blockade failed
The smugglers learn that this route and this cover story work
options.consequence: You let the boat pass so your patrol can keep watching the whole area. You accept that you may have just let a weapons shipment reach the enemy.

costs.resource: a flagged boat let through unsearched
costs.risk: the boat was the shipment, and the cargo you let pass rearms the enemy

entries.event: Your blockade goes up along the coast. Both the smugglers' usual boats and the honest sea traffic are moving.
The smugglers test your coverage. They send a boat through a stretch they think is lightly watched, to learn your patrol pattern.
The smugglers send a decoy boat to pull a patrol away from a real shipment. It is the first clear sign they are reading your moves.
How well the enemy is fighting now shows how much has gotten through. Their ammunition and spare parts are either holding up or starting to run low.
By now it is clear whether your blockade is working. The supply line is either closing or it is not, and the enemy adjusts to match.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Before your contract ends, cut the sea supply line low enough that the enemy can no longer keep fighting. If the weapons keep getting through, the enemy garrison holds out for good, and your blockade has failed at the one thing that matters.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} garrison holds the port, supplied by the smugglers. It defends the port district with 8-11 'Mechs of mixed weight (30-70 tons, Regular quality with a Veteran command lance dug into the waterfront) and a combat-vehicle slice of armor and shore defenses (vehicleShare covers the garrison's vehicles and any escort the smugglers field). The smugglers themselves are small boats and the occasional armed escort, handled as the search-and-stop problem. If a boarding or a shore raid breaks out, the garrison sends a reaction force to protect the landing site. The smuggler crews and the shore ring are infantry and appear only in the story, not on the table.
opforSketch.behavior: The garrison fights to keep its supply line open and to make your blockade expensive. The smugglers use the busy sea, route around your patrols, and send decoys to mislead you. If you strike at a landing, the garrison reacts hard to protect the cargo and the people moving it.

forks.name: OPERATION CLOSED COAST
forks.trigger: The seaborne arms pipeline is cut below the holdouts' sustaining level and their resistance begins to fail.
forks.consequence: Starved of arms, the splinter garrison weakens toward collapse; {EMPLOYER} can move to clear the port against a holdout that can no longer replace what it loses.

forks.name: OPERATION CUT NETWORK
forks.trigger: The shore-side network organizing the runs is identified and rolled up, closing the pipeline for good.
forks.consequence: The pipeline stays shut after the cordon lifts; the captured network exposes the holdouts' off-world suppliers, and the resistance collapses without its lifeline.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN WATER
forks.trigger: The arms keep getting through, or the cordon strangles the population into the holdouts' arms.
forks.consequence: The splinter garrison fights on, resupplied; either the pipeline stayed open or the cordon's heavy hand widened the insurgency, and the port becomes a sore that does not heal.

storyElementSeed: At dusk, a patrol commander watches a low-riding fishing boat head for a shallow channel. She holds its cargo list and remembers an informer's tip. She has to decide: board it and tie up her boat, or keep watching the four other channels that no one else is covering.

phases.name: POSTURE — SETTING THE CORDON
phases.lead: Set up your blockade along a coast too long to watch all at once. Decide how hard to search against how much traffic to leave alone.

dataBlock.Approaches: fishing harbors, cargo docks, and shallow channels, more than your company can cover
dataBlock.Traffic: ordinary coastal boats with smuggled weapons hidden among them
dataBlock.Holdouts: 8-11 'Mechs dug into the port, kept fighting by the smuggled supplies
dataBlock.Intelligence: informer tips and cargo lists, about a day old and seeded with fake tips

sidebarKernel.kernel: which boats the informers flag, which cargo lists do not add up, and how much of it is the smugglers feeding you a false picture.

phases.name: FLASHPOINT — THE INTERCEPT
phases.lead: Read the traffic and act on the boats you suspect. For each one, decide whether to board it, follow it, or let it pass.

routes.name: DEEP CHANNELS
routes.desc: The dredged channels deep enough for large ships.
routes.tradeoff: The heavy weapons must come this way, and you can watch it. But guarding it pulls your patrols off the shallows.

routes.name: TIDAL SHALLOWS
routes.desc: The maze of shallow small-boat channels along the flats.
routes.tradeoff: You cannot cover it all. Small smugglers slip through here, but their boats cannot carry the heavy cargo.

protocol.Board order: Codeword THIN CORDON sends a patrol to stop and search a flagged boat.
protocol.Shadow signal: Codeword SLACK TIDE tells a patrol to follow a smuggler to its landing instead of boarding, so you can find the shore ring.

phases.name: RESOLUTION — CLOSING THE PIPELINE
phases.lead: Over the whole contract, cut the enemy's supplies below what they need to keep fighting. If you can, also track down and arrest the smuggling ring behind the runs.

sidebarKernel.kernel: whether the supply line is closing by the one measure that counts, the enemy running low, and whether you can arrest the shore ring before your contract ends.

assetDetails.detail: The fishermen, cargo crews, and families who live on the water. Choking them to catch the smugglers is exactly the war crime the enemy wants. A blockade that crushes the honest boats around the weapons wins the wrong fight.
Provides the boat flags and cargo-list checks. Warns that the smugglers plant fake tips, and that an obvious, fat-looking boat is just as likely a decoy as a real prize.

title: OPERATION HEAVY LADEN
skeleton: an escort must run a genuinely loaded supply convoy as bait to draw a known raider lance into committing, then spring a hidden heavy element once the raiders are too close to flee, where the cargo is real and must survive the spring rather than being expendable, so the trap has to be sold convincingly without sacrificing the load it is built around, against former-comrade raiders who know the escort's tactics
inspiration: the convoy-as-bait anti-raider trap, but with a real cargo that must come through - the loaded-decoy problem of contested commerce protection
situation: For three weeks, a {TARGET_FACTION} raider lance has been hitting {EMPLOYER}'s supply convoys in {DISTRICT}. The only way to stop them is to offer a convoy they cannot resist. The catch is that this convoy carries real supplies, and those supplies have to arrive. The raiders operate on {WORLD}, and success has made them bold and predictable. They attack lightly escorted convoys out on the open stretches of road. They grab what they can carry, then pull out before any reaction force can reach them. {EMPLOYER} wants to end this by setting a trap, and your company is the trap. You will run a convoy that looks rich and lightly guarded, tempting enough that the raiders commit to attacking it. When they close in, a hidden heavy element in the column and along the route springs and pins them where they cannot escape. The hard part is that this is not an empty decoy. The convoy carries fuel and ammunition that the forward force truly needs, and {EMPLOYER} cannot spare empty trucks for a trick or afford to lose the load. So the bait has to look like real cargo, survive the attack, and reach its destination while the hidden heavy element kills the raiders around it. The raiders are not strangers. They were {EMPLOYER}'s own scouts before they defected. They know how this company guards a convoy, where it puts its lookouts, and how its escort reacts when attacked. You are trying to fool people who learned these tactics alongside you. Your best guess at where they will strike comes from their last three attacks. It is a useful pattern, not a certainty, because raiders this careful may spot the trap.

objectives.primary: Lure the {TARGET_FACTION} raider lance into attacking the bait convoy, then use the hidden heavy element to destroy it or break it as a fighting force.
objectives.secondary: Bring the real cargo through the ambush intact and delivered to the forward force.
objectives.bonus: Capture the raiders' 'Mechs intact instead of destroying them, so you recover the machines that have been raiding the convoys.

complications.name: The Bait Is the Prize
complications.text: This is not an empty decoy. The convoy carries fuel and ammunition that the forward force needs and {EMPLOYER} cannot replace. So the trap has to close without destroying the cargo. The cargo sits right in the middle of the ambush and still has to survive it. Killing the raiders but wrecking the convoy counts as only half a win.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The convoy vehicles carry real, valuable cargo you must protect during the fight. Every convoy vehicle lost during the ambush costs you the secondary objective. So the heavy element has to kill the raiders without its own crossfire destroying the cargo.

complications.name: They Wrote the Playbook
complications.text: The raiders were your side's scouts a month ago. They know how this company guards a convoy, where it posts lookouts, and how its escort reacts when attacked. If your ambush looks like the standard escort setup, they may recognize it, because they helped create that setup.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The enemy compares the convoy to the escort tactics they already know. If you use the standard setup, the raiders are more likely to sense the trap and refuse to attack. Changing the setup convincingly hides the trap but takes extra time and effort to prepare.

complications.name: Reading the Bait for the Hook
complications.text: The raiders stay alive by watching their targets closely, and a convoy that looks too perfect makes them suspicious. Reveal the heavy element too early and the raiders pull back before you can pin them. Reveal it too late and they have already damaged the convoy and escaped. You have only a short window to get the timing right.
complications.mechanicalEffect: You have only a narrow window to spring the trap. Trigger it too early and the raiders break off before they are committed to the attack. Trigger it too late and they damage the convoy and escape. You must spring it in the short gap after the raiders commit but before they can flee.

decisionPoints.name: How to Sell the Convoy
decisionPoints.context: The bait only works if the raiders believe it is real. How you set up the convoy decides two things: whether they attack, and whether they notice the trap.

options.title: Standard escort, look routine
advantages: A familiar setup looks like an ordinary, tempting target
Needs no special preparation
Looks exactly like the convoys the raiders keep attacking
disadvantages: The raiders know this setup well and may spot the trap
A standard escort gives the heavy element few places to hide
The same predictability that tempts them can also warn them
options.consequence: You run the convoy the way the raiders expect. You are betting that the familiar look tempts them more than it warns them.

costs.resource: a trap that uses the standard escort setup
costs.risk: the raiders recognize their old tactics and refuse to take the bait

options.title: Thin the visible escort, hide the weight
advantages: A lightly guarded convoy looks like an easy target
Hides the heavy element completely, away from the convoy
Gives the raiders the strongest reason to attack
disadvantages: A thin visible escort cannot protect the cargo if the trap fails
The hidden force must move fast to reach and pin the raiders
If the heavy element arrives late, the convoy takes the hit alone
options.consequence: You make the convoy look weak. You are betting the hidden force closes the trap before the thin escort pays for the deception.

costs.resource: the convoy's visible guards cut to a minimum
costs.risk: the hidden force is slow and the lightly guarded cargo is torn apart before the trap closes

options.title: Stage a believable weakness
advantages: A faked breakdown or straggler makes the convoy look vulnerable and real
Draws the raiders toward a spot you have already prepared
A believable flaw is more convincing than a target that looks perfect
disadvantages: If the raiders see through the fake weakness, it warns them the trap is there
Ties the fight to one prepared spot the raiders may avoid
Faking a flaw convincingly takes skill and discipline
options.consequence: You show the raiders a weak point to attack and spring the trap when they go for it. You are betting the flaw looks like bad luck, not a lure.

costs.resource: a fake weakness committed to one location
costs.risk: the raiders see the fake weakness as a trap and attack somewhere else or not at all

decisionPoints.name: The Raiders Commit
decisionPoints.context: The raider lance moves in on the convoy. You choose when to spring the trap: too early lets them escape, too late costs you the cargo. How hard you fight them decides whether you destroy their 'Mechs or capture them intact.

options.title: Spring hard, kill them fast
advantages: Pins the raiders and destroys them before they can break away
Keeps the convoy under enemy fire for as little time as possible
Almost certainly destroys the threat
disadvantages: A hard, fast kill risks catching the convoy in the crossfire
You destroy the raiders' 'Mechs, so you cannot capture them intact
Heavy fighting happens right next to the cargo you must protect
options.consequence: You close the trap with full force. You accept that a fast, certain kill may leave the cargo with some damage.

costs.resource: the raiders' 'Mechs destroyed instead of captured
costs.risk: the crossfire that kills the raiders also damages the cargo

options.title: Pin and force surrender
advantages: Cornered raiders may surrender, handing over their 'Mechs intact
Spares the convoy a destructive close-range fight
Recovers the machines that have been raiding the convoys
disadvantages: A cornered raider who refuses to surrender fights hardest
Offering surrender terms takes time, and the convoy stays exposed
Former comrades may choose death over capture by their old unit
options.consequence: You surround them and offer them a way to live. You are betting they surrender before the standoff turns into a close fight over the cargo.

costs.resource: time spent forcing a surrender
costs.risk: the raiders refuse to surrender and the drawn-out fight still endangers the convoy

options.title: Protect the cargo first, kill second
advantages: Puts the heavy element between the raiders and the convoy first
Makes sure the cargo gets through
Trades a clean kill for a safe delivery
disadvantages: Fighting defensively lets some raiders break off and escape
The surviving raiders may go on to hit another convoy
Putting the cargo first gives up the chance to destroy the whole lance
options.consequence: You protect the cargo and let the trap be less than perfect. You accept that some raiders escape so the cargo arrives safely.

costs.resource: some raiders allowed to escape to protect the cargo
costs.risk: the surviving raiders regroup and the convoy problem is not solved

entries.event: The bait convoy sets out on the open stretch. The heavy element is hidden in the column and along the route.
The raiders' scouts spot the convoy and follow it, deciding whether it is an easy target or a trap.
The raider lance moves into a strike position, comparing the escort to the tactics they already know.
The raiders commit to the attack. This opens the short window in which you can spring the trap.
The fight is decided. The raiders are pinned, broken, or gone, and the convoy is intact or damaged.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Spring the trap after the raiders commit but before they can flee. If you miss that window, one of two things happens. The raiders spot the trap and escape unharmed, or they hit the convoy and break away with the cargo you were sworn to protect.

opforSketch.composition: A fast, experienced {TARGET_FACTION} raider lance. It has 4-6 light and medium 'Mechs (25-55 tons, Veteran, former scouts who know friendly escort tactics) built for hit-and-run attacks. A few fast combat vehicles back them up, hauling loot and screening (vehicleShare covers the raiders' transport and scout vehicles). They attack lightly escorted convoys and break off before a reaction force can reach them. They compare each target to the escort tactics they helped create and refuse anything that looks like a trap. Once committed, they fight hard, but they run the moment the odds turn against them unless they are pinned against terrain.
opforSketch.behavior: Bold from repeated success and sharp from experience. The raiders study their targets, hit the weak and the predictable, and stay alive by avoiding any fight they did not choose. Their biggest strength is also their biggest weakness: they know the convoy's tactics because those tactics used to be their own.

forks.name: OPERATION SPRUNG TRAP
forks.trigger: The raider lance is destroyed or broken and the real cargo comes through intact.
forks.consequence: The convoys run safe again and the forward force gets its supply; {EMPLOYER}'s commerce in the district is freed of the predator that was bleeding it.

forks.name: OPERATION FULL BAG
forks.trigger: The raider lance is taken largely intact as salvage and the cargo is delivered whole.
forks.consequence: Not only is the threat ended, the recovered 'Mechs reinforce {EMPLOYER}'s own line; the captured raiders' knowledge of the district's routes becomes an intelligence windfall.

forks.name: OPERATION SMELLED THE HOOK
forks.trigger: The raiders decline the bait having read the trap, or strike the convoy and break contact before the spring closes.
forks.consequence: The raider lance survives, wiser to the tactic, and either the cargo is lost or the trap is blown for good; the convoys stay prey and the forward force does without what the bait was carrying.

storyElementSeed: An escort commander rides in a heavy, slow hauler down the open road, showing only a thin guard on purpose. Her hidden lances wait in silence on the radio. She knows the raiders about to take her bait once stood the same watch she does now.

phases.name: INGRESS — RUNNING THE BAIT
phases.lead: Send the bait convoy down the road where the raiders hunt, and set it up to tempt people who know your tactics.

dataBlock.Bait: a convoy carrying real cargo that cannot be replaced
dataBlock.Hook: a heavy element hidden in the column and along the route
dataBlock.Quarry: a raider lance of 4-6 'Mechs, all former friendly scouts
dataBlock.Pattern: the raiders' last three attacks, which are a guide but not a guarantee

sidebarKernel.kernel: where the raiders' pattern says they will strike, and whether the convoy looks like an easy target or like a trap.

phases.name: GROUND — THE COMMIT
phases.lead: Draw the raiders into attacking, then spring the hidden heavy element in the short window before they can flee.

routes.name: OPEN STRETCH
routes.desc: The exposed road where the raiders like to attack.
routes.tradeoff: Tempting bait ground, but so open that the raiders can break off fast if you spring the trap too slowly.

routes.name: CHOKE GROUND
routes.desc: Where the route narrows between terrain.
routes.tradeoff: Good for pinning the raiders where they cannot escape, but a spot they may be too cautious to enter.

protocol.Spring trigger: The codeword HEAVY LADEN reveals the hidden element the moment the raiders are committed to the attack.
protocol.Cargo-cover call: The codeword KEEP THE LOAD orders the heavy element to protect the convoy instead of chasing a kill.

phases.name: EXTRACTION — THROUGH THE AMBUSH
phases.lead: Finish off the raiders and bring the cargo through the ambush ground, choosing whether to chase a kill or guard the cargo.

sidebarKernel.kernel: whether the raiders are pinned, broken, or running, and whether the cargo can get through undamaged while the heavy element finishes the fight.

assetDetails.detail: Fuel and ammunition the forward force needs and {EMPLOYER} cannot replace. It is both the bait and the prize. A trap that wins but destroys the cargo has only half succeeded.
Former friendly scouts who know the escort tactics. That knowledge makes the trap hard to sell, and it makes their 'Mechs worth capturing intact.

title: OPERATION KEYSTONE
skeleton: a force must seize and hold intact the demolition firing-point of the one grand viaduct its own offensive needs to cross, while the defender's whole plan is to drop the span, and the failure-tempting easy out is to blow it for denial - so the crux is taking the firing-point before the charges go and refusing the order that would make the prize useless, against a garrison fighting to deny the crossing rather than to survive
inspiration: the race to seize the Ludendorff railway bridge at Remagen before the defenders could demolish it, 1945
situation: Only one bridge in {DISTRICT} can carry a 'Mech army across the gorge. Whoever holds it intact controls how fast this campaign moves. That bridge is the great viaduct over the gorge on {WORLD}. It is the only crossing rated for assault tonnage for two hundred kilometers in either direction. The gorge below is a sheer drop. No 'Mech can ford it, and no light bridge can span it. {EMPLOYER}'s offensive is driving toward this crossing, and that advance only works if the viaduct stands. The {TARGET_FACTION} garrison holding the far end knows this too. Its plan is simple: wire the span with explosives and drop it the moment your advance commits to crossing. That trades the bridge for weeks of delay, because {EMPLOYER}'s army then stalls at a gorge it cannot cross. Your company must take the viaduct before the garrison can fire the charges. That means seizing the demolition firing-point at the far abutment. Cut the wires to the charges, or hold the firing gallery so no one can trigger them. Keep the span whole and open for the army coming up behind you. One easy option will tempt every officer here. If you cannot take the firing-point in time, you could blow the bridge yourself to deny it to the enemy. Do not. Blowing it yourself fails the mission just as badly as letting the enemy blow it. A dropped bridge stops {EMPLOYER}'s offensive either way, no matter whose hand pulls the trigger. Your map of the charges and the firing-point comes from an engineer reading aerial photos. That read is only hours old, and the enemy may have moved the trigger since it was made. So you are racing the enemy to the trigger across a bridge you must keep intact. The worst outcome is the enemy blowing it. The only thing as bad is you blowing it for them.

objectives.primary: Seize the viaduct's demolition firing-point and secure the span intact and usable, before the {TARGET_FACTION} garrison can blow it.
objectives.secondary: Hold the far end of the bridge and keep the crossing open until {EMPLOYER}'s lead units are across.
objectives.bonus: Capture the enemy demolition team and their charge plan intact. That lets you clear every explosive off the span and hold it with no fear of a hidden delayed trigger.

complications.name: The Hand on the Trigger
complications.text: The span is wired, and the garrison plans to fire it the instant your advance commits. So everything depends on reaching the firing-point before the enemy commander gives the order to blow it. A loud, slow approach only warns them. The same alarm that announces you is the alarm that fires the charges.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The demolition trigger arms once the garrison sees a committed assault on the bridge. Seizing the firing-point or cutting the demolition wires before it fires is a hard timed sub-objective. Fail it and the span drops, which fails the offensive too.

complications.name: The Easy Out
complications.text: If you cannot take the firing-point in time, any officer can end the suspense by blowing the bridge first to deny it to the enemy. That may feel decisive, but it is still a failure. A gorge with no bridge stops {EMPLOYER}'s army just as hard, no matter who dropped it. The temptation grows with every minute the firing-point holds out.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Blowing the bridge yourself is always an option, and in the moment it looks like a denial win. But it gives up the primary objective and the crossing the offensive needs. The mission rewards holding the span whole, not destroying it.

complications.name: Fighting to Deny, Not to Live
complications.text: The garrison is not fighting to survive. It is fighting to make sure no one crosses. That changes how it behaves. It will take heavy losses without flinching, just to buy the seconds the demolition needs. A defender that does not care about its own losses will not break when a normal one would.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The OpFor fights to deny the crossing, not to preserve itself. It does not retreat at the usual damage thresholds. It will trade heavily to protect the firing-point and buy the demolition team its window to fire.

decisionPoints.name: How to Take the Firing-Point
decisionPoints.context: The charges arm the moment the garrison sees a committed assault. How you go for the firing-point decides whether you beat the enemy to the trigger.

options.title: Coup de main across the span
advantages: A fast element rushes straight across to the far abutment and the firing-point
Best chance to reach the trigger before it is pressed
Takes the bridge by speed before the defense can react
disadvantages: You are rushing across a span rigged with live explosives
If the charges fire, the lead element is out there alone and exposed
You commit to the bridge before the far end is suppressed
options.consequence: You sprint the span and bet that speed beats the enemy's finger on the trigger. Everything rides on the lead element.

costs.resource: the lead element, staked on a rush across the wired span
costs.risk: the charges fire mid-rush, dropping the lead element into the gorge with the bridge

options.title: Infiltrate the firing-point first
advantages: A small infiltration element cuts the demolition lines before the assault commits
Disarms the trigger without announcing a full attack
If it works, the bridge is taken without a race at all
disadvantages: Infiltration takes time and the charge layout may have moved
A blown infiltration arms the very trigger it meant to cut
Rests on hours-old intelligence about where the lines run
options.consequence: You try to quietly cut the demolition wires before the main fight starts. You are gambling that the charges are where the engineers think they are.

costs.resource: time for a quiet approach to the firing-point
costs.risk: the infiltration is discovered and the alarm fires the charges early

options.title: Suppress the far end, then cross
advantages: Beats down the abutment defenses with fire before committing to the span
Lowers the risk to the assault element on the crossing
Methodical and survivable if the trigger holds
disadvantages: Suppression takes time the demolition party uses to fire the charges
A deliberate buildup is the committed assault that arms the trigger
Trades speed for safety against a clock that punishes slowness
options.consequence: You soften the far end properly and gamble the extra minutes do not give the enemy the window to drop the span.

costs.resource: minutes spent suppressing while the trigger stands armed
costs.risk: the deliberate approach gives the demolition party the time it needs and the bridge falls

decisionPoints.name: The Firing-Point Holds Out
decisionPoints.context: Time is running out and the firing-point is still not yours. The enemy may fire at any second. You can press the assault, hold and call the army forward, or take the easy way out and blow the bridge yourself.

options.title: Press the assault on the trigger
advantages: Keeps fighting for the only outcome that wins - an intact bridge
A pressed assault may yet reach the firing-point in time
Refuses to do the enemy's demolition for him
disadvantages: Every minute pressing is a minute the charges might fire
Heavy casualties against a defender spending itself to deny
May reach the trigger only to find it already pressed
options.consequence: You keep driving for the firing-point because a whole bridge is the mission, and accept the cost of racing a detonator.

costs.resource: the company spent racing the trigger
costs.risk: the charges fire while you press and the bridge falls with your lead element on it

options.title: Hold and rush the army forward
advantages: Buys the firing-point fight more weight by hurrying {EMPLOYER}'s lead across
More force on the far end may overwhelm the demolition party
Keeps the crossing as the goal
disadvantages: Rushing the army onto a wired bridge risks losing the lead elements with it
Coordinating the hurry takes time the trigger may not give
Stakes more of the offensive on a span that may still drop
options.consequence: You pull the whole offensive forward onto the gamble and double the stakes on the bridge holding.

costs.resource: the offensive's lead committed to the wired span
costs.risk: the bridge drops with {EMPLOYER}'s lead elements crossing it

options.title: Blow the bridge yourself
advantages: Ends the uncertainty and denies the crossing to the enemy
Stops a {TARGET_FACTION} counterattack from using the span
Feels like a clean decision under fire
disadvantages: Forfeits the offensive's only crossing for two hundred kilometers
Stops {EMPLOYER}'s army exactly as dead as an enemy demolition would
Turns the whole operation into a self-inflicted failure
options.consequence: You take the easy way out. A bridge you blew yourself is still a bridge your army cannot cross.

costs.resource: the crossing the offensive needs, destroyed
costs.risk: the dropped span halts {EMPLOYER}'s entire advance, and the campaign loses its momentum

entries.event: The company reaches the near end of the bridge. The span is wired, and the firing-point at the far end is manned.
The garrison reads your approach as an attack and readies the demolition charges to fire.
The race for the firing-point is on. Your lead element is on the span or closing on it.
Under pressure, the demolition team gets ready to fire on their commander's order rather than lose the bridge intact.
It ends one of two ways. Either you take the firing-point and hold the span whole, or the charges fire and the span drops into the gorge.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Seize the firing-point and secure the span before the garrison fires the charges. Once the bridge drops, whether by their hand or yours, the offensive has lost its crossing. That is mission failure, plain and simple.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} bridge garrison fighting to deny the crossing, not to survive. It has 8-11 'Mechs of mixed weight (35-70 tons, Regular quality with a Veteran command lance), dug in at the far end to cover the firing-point. Combat vehicles back them up as armor and as guards for the demolition team (vehicleShare covers the far-end vehicles and gate defenses). The 'Mechs hold the far end and the routes to the firing-point. They will take heavy losses to buy the demolition team its window to fire. The demolition team itself is infantry and is handled in the story rather than on the board, but its trigger is the central threat of the mission. The garrison does not break at the usual damage thresholds. Its job is to win those seconds, not to survive.
opforSketch.behavior: This is a denial defense: stop anyone from crossing intact. The garrison holds the firing-point, buys the demolition team the moment it needs, and trades lives to make sure no one gets across. It fights hardest right at the trigger. It is counting on the attacker being too slow, or on the attacker blowing the bridge himself.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN CROSSING
forks.trigger: The firing-point is seized and the span is held intact and trafficable while {EMPLOYER}'s lead elements cross.
forks.consequence: The offensive pours across the gorge on schedule; {EMPLOYER} holds the campaign's tempo and the far bank, and the viaduct becomes the artery of the advance.

forks.name: OPERATION CLEAN SPAN
forks.trigger: The demolition party and the charge plan are captured intact and the span is cleared of explosives.
forks.consequence: The bridge is not only held but proven safe; {EMPLOYER} crosses without fear of a delayed trigger and turns the secured viaduct into a permanent crossing for the whole campaign.

forks.name: OPERATION DROPPED SPAN
forks.trigger: The charges fire - by the enemy's hand or by the company taking the easy out - and the span goes into the gorge.
forks.consequence: The offensive's only crossing is gone for two hundred kilometers; {EMPLOYER}'s army stalls at an uncrossable gorge for weeks, and the campaign's tempo dies with the bridge.

storyElementSeed: A lance commander stares across the wired span at the gallery where an enemy demolition team waits for one word to fire. His own hand rests near his firing key. He knows the easy choice and the right choice are opposites here.

phases.name: INGRESS — THE NEAR ABUTMENT
phases.lead: Reach the viaduct and choose how to go for the firing-point before the garrison can fire the charges.

dataBlock.Crossing: the only span rated for assault tonnage for 200 km, spanning a sheer gorge
dataBlock.Threat to the prize: the span is wired with explosives, and the garrison plans to blow it
dataBlock.Far-end defense: 8-11 'Mechs and combat vehicles covering the firing-point
dataBlock.Charge intelligence: an engineer's read from aerial photos, only hours old and possibly out of date

sidebarKernel.kernel: our best guess at where the charges and demolition wires are, and whether you can reach or cut the firing-point before the enemy presses the trigger.

phases.name: GROUND — RACING THE TRIGGER
phases.lead: Drive for the firing-point and secure the span whole. Do not take the easy way out and blow it yourself.

routes.name: THE DECK
routes.desc: The span itself, straight across to the far end.
routes.tradeoff: The fastest way to the firing-point. But if the charges fire, you are on top of the explosives.

routes.name: GORGE PATH
routes.desc: A steep route up to the far end that stays off the span.
routes.tradeoff: It keeps you off the wired deck, but the slow ground costs time you may not have.

protocol.Firing-point secure: Codeword KEYSTONE means the demolition trigger is taken or cut, and the span is now safe.
protocol.Hold-fire discipline: Codeword WHOLE SPAN forbids any friendly demolition of the bridge. Hold the crossing, do not destroy it.

phases.name: EXTRACTION — HOLDING IT OPEN
phases.lead: Hold the far end and keep the crossing open until the army is across. Decide how much you are willing to spend if the firing-point fight drags on.

sidebarKernel.kernel: whether the firing-point is secured, whether the lead units are crossing, and whether anyone still wants to blow the bridge.

assetDetails.detail: The only crossing rated for assault tonnage for 200 km. Held intact, it keeps the campaign moving. Dropped, it stalls {EMPLOYER}'s army for weeks. The whole operation is the fight to keep it whole.
The enemy engineers who can blow the bridge, fighting to buy the seconds they need to fire. Capturing them and their charge plan is the difference between a held bridge and a truly safe one.

title: OPERATION CLOSED MOUTH
skeleton: a deniable element must cripple the enemy theater's logistics-coordination relay so a wider offensive lands on a blinded foe, leaving no proof of who did it, where the relay is a dual-use civilian node and an open attack on it is an atrocity the employer cannot own, so the crux is creating the blackout and walking away clean rather than the demolition itself
inspiration: deniable sabotage of an enemy's command-and-coordination node ahead of an offensive, with attribution as the binding constraint
situation: {EMPLOYER} is about to launch an offensive. It will only work if the enemy cannot see it coming. On {WORLD}, the {TARGET_FACTION} command in {DISTRICT} runs its supply and its reaction forces through one regional signal-relay. That relay ties a scattered garrison together. It routes resupply, sends reaction orders, and tracks where every enemy unit is. Cripple it and the enemy's response breaks into a dozen small, uncoordinated fights. Then {EMPLOYER}'s main attack lands on a foe that cannot pull itself together. But {EMPLOYER} cannot be seen touching this relay. The catch is what else it does. It also carries the district's civilian traffic - emergency calls, hospital links, everyday business. An open military strike on it would kill those services too, which the other side would call an atrocity. That propaganda would hurt {EMPLOYER} more than the offensive helps. So this job must be deniable. Your team goes in with no unit markings, cripples only the military side of the relay, and makes it look like an accident or the work of unknown saboteurs. Deniability is the mission, not a bonus. A strike that works but gets traced to {EMPLOYER} fails just as badly as a strike that does nothing. Your only map is a diagram from a technician who defected. It is two days old. Cut the wrong line and you black out a hospital instead of a battalion.

objectives.primary: Cripple the military side of the {TARGET_FACTION} regional signal-relay so the enemy cannot pull its forces together against {EMPLOYER}'s coming offensive.
objectives.secondary: Leave no proof that {EMPLOYER} did it. The strike must look like an accident or the work of unknown saboteurs.
objectives.bonus: Leave the relay's civilian traffic working. Cripple only the military side, so the blackout kills no civilian services the enemy could use against you.

complications.name: Fingerprints Are the Failure
complications.text: If the enemy can prove {EMPLOYER} took down the relay, that is worse than not striking at all. It gives the other side proof of an attack on civilian services, and the propaganda that comes with it. So the goal is not just to break the relay. The goal is to break it without leaving any trace of who did it.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Any evidence that points back to you turns a working strike into a strategic loss. That includes captured gear in your colors, a 'Mech fight someone sees, or a recognizable unit signature. Deniability is a hard pass-or-fail on top of the demolition: leave proof and the mission fails no matter how well the relay went down.

complications.name: The Glass House
complications.text: The relay carries the district's civilian services alongside the enemy's military traffic - emergency lines, hospital links, everyday calls. The two run through the same building, often the same lines, sometimes the same hardware. Cut the wrong one and you black out a hospital. That is exactly the atrocity you were sent to prevent.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The military and civilian systems are tangled together. A crude or rushed strike damages the civilian side. That causes the civilian harm and the propaganda the deniable plan exists to avoid, and it forfeits the bonus.

complications.name: Two Days Stale
complications.text: Your only map is a defector's diagram, and it is two days old. A relay like this gets rewired often. The part you came to cut may have moved, been hardened, or been split in two. If you find that out inside the building with the clock running, that is the moment a quiet job turns loud.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The diagram may be out of date. If the layout has changed, your team has to improvise inside the building. That takes more time on target and raises the risk of a noisy strike that gets traced back to you.

decisionPoints.name: How to Cripple the Relay
decisionPoints.context: You can knock out the relay several ways, but only some stay deniable and spare the civilian traffic. Your method decides what the enemy finds afterward.

options.title: Surgical sabotage of the coordination core
advantages: Cuts only the military side and leaves the civilian traffic working
Looks like equipment failure or sabotage no one can pin on you
The cleanest result on all three objectives
disadvantages: You have to reach the core deep inside a guarded building
It only works if the two-day-old diagram is still right about what to cut
The work is slow and delicate, and the clock is running
options.consequence: You go for one clean cut. The whole job rides on the diagram being right and your hand staying steady inside the building.

costs.resource: time for slow, delicate work deep inside the building
costs.risk: the core has been rewired, the precise cut fails, and you are forced into a loud improvisation

options.title: Stage an accident
advantages: A faked power surge or fire looks like an accident, not an attack
The best deniability of any option, if the staging holds
No 'Mech fight for anyone to see or trace
disadvantages: A staged accident is hard to control and may take the civilian traffic down with it
An investigator who sees through it can pin the attack on you anyway
It needs setup and skill the team may not have under pressure
options.consequence: You make the relay's failure look like bad luck. You are betting the staging fools whoever examines the wreckage.

costs.resource: specialist staging crew committed
costs.risk: the accident reads as sabotage instead, and it damages the civilian services as well

options.title: Cut the external lines, leave the building
advantages: Cuts the relay's reach without entering the guarded building
The lowest chance of anyone seeing a fight at the site
Fast, looks fixable, and hard to trace
disadvantages: Cut lines get repaired faster than a wrecked core
May not separate the military traffic from the civilian traffic
A shorter blackout that may not last through the offensive
options.consequence: You choke the relay from outside. You accept a shorter, weaker blackout in exchange for a cleaner, safer job.

costs.resource: a shorter, weaker blackout in exchange for a clean exit
costs.risk: the lines are repaired before the offensive lands and the enemy gets its coordination back in time

decisionPoints.name: The Job Turns Loud
decisionPoints.context: Inside, the layout is not what the diagram showed, and a guard patrol is closing in. You can finish the precise cut and risk being found, fall back to a crude strike that blacks out everything, or break off to protect deniability.

options.title: Finish the clean cut under pressure
advantages: Still gives the clean, deniable result if it works
Leaves the civilian traffic working, as planned
Saves all three objectives from a bad moment
disadvantages: Staying while a patrol closes risks a fight someone sees
A fight at the relay destroys your deniability
Delicate work is hardest when you are rushing
options.consequence: You stay to finish the clean cut. You are betting you can finish and slip away before the patrol turns the job into evidence.

costs.resource: your deniability, staked on beating the patrol
costs.risk: the patrol arrives mid-cut and the fight hands the enemy proof it was you

options.title: Crude strike, take the whole relay
advantages: Makes sure the military traffic goes down
Fast, and done before the patrol can step in
Hits the primary objective for certain
disadvantages: Blacks out the civilian traffic too, causing the atrocity
A wrecked relay is clearly an attack, not an accident
Forfeits both the deniability and the bonus
options.consequence: You wreck the whole thing to be sure. In doing so you hand the enemy the civilian blackout, and the propaganda, you were meant to avoid.

costs.resource: both the deniability and the spared civilian traffic, given up
costs.risk: the crude strike gets traced to {EMPLOYER}, and the harm to civilians becomes the enemy's win

options.title: Break off to stay clean
advantages: Protects your deniability, which matters more than the strike
No fight anyone sees, and no evidence left behind
Keeps the door open to try again another way
disadvantages: The relay survives and the enemy keeps its coordination
The offensive then lands on a foe that can still pull together
An aborted job is a job left undone
options.consequence: You pull out clean and accept that the enemy can still see. You are betting an offensive against an alert enemy beats one blamed on you.

costs.resource: the strike given up to protect deniability
costs.risk: the offensive hits a coordinated enemy and pays the price the strike was meant to spare it

entries.event: The team reaches the relay with no unit markings. Inside, the relay is carrying both military and civilian traffic.
The team makes its approach or entry and sees how the real layout differs from the two-day-old diagram.
The team locates the military side of the relay, either where the diagram said or wherever it has been moved to.
A guard patrol comes around toward the relay. The window for quiet work starts to close.
The strike goes in and the team slips away clean, or the job has turned loud and can be traced back to you.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Cripple the military side of the relay and be gone, untraceable, before the offensive is committed. Two things fail the mission: a relay still coordinating the enemy when the main attack lands, or a strike that gets traced to {EMPLOYER}.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} relay security detachment, light and not expecting a 'Mech-scale threat. It has a guard force of 3-5 light 'Mechs (20-45 tons, Regular) and a security-vehicle slice patrolling the perimeter (vehicleShare carries the patrol vehicles and gate defenses), plus a reaction element that comes if the relay is openly attacked. The guard is built to stop saboteurs and intruders, not to win a stand-up fight. Its real value to the enemy is as witnesses: if you fight them, they can prove it was {EMPLOYER}, which is the one thing you must avoid. The relay staff and any investigators are infantry and appear in the story, but being seen is the true danger here.
opforSketch.behavior: A routine security posture. They patrol on a set cycle, alert for intruders but not braced for an assault. Their danger is not firepower but their eyes. Any fight with them turns a deniable job into proof, so treat them as a threat to slip past and outrun rather than one to fight.

forks.name: OPERATION DEAF GARRISON
forks.trigger: The relay's coordination function is crippled and the strike stays unattributable.
forks.consequence: The enemy's reaction falls into uncoordinated local fights and {EMPLOYER}'s offensive lands on a foe that cannot mass; no one can prove who closed the relay's mouth.

forks.name: OPERATION CLEAN HANDS
forks.trigger: Only the military function is killed, the civilian traffic is spared, and nothing traces back to {EMPLOYER}.
forks.consequence: The blackout carries no humanitarian cost for the enemy to exploit and no fingerprints to follow; {EMPLOYER} reaps a blinded enemy and a clean conscience, and the tactic stays available for reuse.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN SECRET
forks.trigger: The strike is traced to {EMPLOYER}, or it blacks out the civilian nets, or the relay survives to coordinate the enemy's response.
forks.consequence: Either the enemy masses against the offensive with its coordination intact, or {EMPLOYER} is handed the blame for an attack on civilian infrastructure; the propaganda or the coordinated defense costs more than the strike was ever worth.

storyElementSeed: A specialist crouches in the relay's humming equipment hall. In one hand she holds a defector's two-day-old diagram, in the other a wire cutter. One line carries a battalion's orders; another carries a city's emergency calls. She has time to be sure of only one before she cuts.

title: OPERATION LAST SAILING
skeleton: an evacuation force must lift thousands of pro-loyalist dependents and a fuel-short mixed column off a world flipping sides, with sealift and dropship capacity metered far below the need, paced by the slowest evacuees and a fuel floor it cannot refill, against former-allied pursuit, where the cruelty is choosing who makes the lift and who is left to the side that is turning
inspiration: the mass evacuation under collapse and the lift-capacity triage of Dunkirk, 1940
situation: This world is switching sides, and you have ships for only a fraction of the people who backed the side that is losing. When the garrison of {WORLD} declared for {TARGET_FACTION}, it stranded thousands of pro-loyalist dependents - the families of officers who stayed loyal, the administrators, and the workers from {EMPLOYER}'s sites in {DISTRICT}. They are trapped on a planet turning hostile around them. {EMPLOYER} has sent all the ships it could gather and your company to protect them, but the numbers are brutal: the dropships and the hired sealift can carry only some of the people who need out. The rest will be left to a side that is settling scores. Your job is to run the evacuation. Hold the loading point, organize the crowd, and get the ships loaded and away. You must also bring out {EMPLOYER}'s remaining military column. That column runs only on the fuel already in its tanks, because the enemy holds the fuel depots now and there is no way to refuel. The evacuation moves at the speed of its slowest people: the old, the injured, the children, and families carrying everything they own. The pursuit moves faster. That pursuit is the former garrison - allies a week ago. They know {EMPLOYER}'s units, faces, and habits, and they are closing on the loading point to stop the lift and seize what they can. Your intelligence on how fast they are coming, and how many ships will actually show up, is a rough guess that gets worse as the operation runs. You will fill every ship and still turn people away at the ramp, all while your fuel runs low and a pursuit you once fought beside comes up the road behind you.

objectives.primary: Hold the loading point and get out as many pro-loyalist dependents as the ships can carry before the pursuit takes it.
objectives.secondary: Get {EMPLOYER}'s military column out with the evacuation, using only the fuel it has, since it cannot refuel.
objectives.bonus: Get out the highest-priority evacuees - the officers' families and key administrators the turning side most wants - even as the general lift fills up and runs out of room.

complications.name: Not Enough Hulls
complications.text: The ships can carry only a fraction of the people who need to leave. Every ship that fills and flies leaves a crowd behind at the ramp. You will organize the crowd, decide who has priority, and turn the rest away. The people you turn away are left to a side that is settling scores. There is no way for everyone to get out.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Ship capacity is fixed and far smaller than the number of evacuees. You must openly decide who boards. The number you get out is limited by how many ships arrive and how long you hold the loading point.

complications.name: The Falling Gauge
complications.text: The military column runs only on the fuel already in its tanks, because the enemy holds the fuel depots now and there is no way to refuel. Every move to protect the evacuation and every reposition against the pursuit burns fuel the column cannot replace. Protect the lift too hard and the column will not have enough fuel left to reach the ships itself.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The column has a fixed amount of fuel that drops with every move and every fight. Spending it to protect the evacuation may leave the column unable to reach the loading point, which means abandoning some of its units.

complications.name: Allies Last Week
complications.text: The pursuit is the former garrison - units that fought beside {EMPLOYER} just a week ago. They know the column's makeup, its officers, its habits, and its faces. They are not guessing how the evacuation will move. They remember. And some of them want the people on those ramps badly enough to push hard for the loading point.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Because they served alongside your force, the enemy can predict how the evacuation will move and press the loading point on a set timeline. Their familiarity strips away the guesswork a normal pursuit would face.

decisionPoints.name: How to Run the Lift
decisionPoints.context: There are more people than ship space, and less time than people. How you organize the crowd decides who gets out and who is still at the ramp when it closes.

options.title: First come, fill and fly
advantages: The fastest loading - ships fly as soon as they are full
Gets the largest raw number of people out
No time lost to sorting the crowd
disadvantages: The weakest and the most important people may never reach the front
A panicked crowd at the ramp is hard to control
Who gets out is left to chance and to who is standing closest
options.consequence: You move as many people as you can and let the crowd sort itself. You are choosing total numbers over who those people are.

costs.resource: no sorting - whoever is closest boards
costs.risk: the important and the helpless get left behind while the fit and the lucky fill the ships

options.title: Triage by priority
advantages: Gets the most important and the most endangered out first
Keeps faith with the people the turning side most wants
A controlled, orderly loading order you can defend
disadvantages: Sorting the crowd eats up precious loading time
Fewer people get out overall as the clock burns on sorting
Turning away the able-bodied to load the helpless is its own hard scene
options.consequence: You load by who needs it most and matters most. You accept that the sorting costs you people the clock could have carried.

costs.resource: loading time spent sorting the crowd
costs.risk: the loading point falls mid-sort and fewer people get out than a first-come rush would have carried

options.title: Two streams, military last
advantages: Loads the dependents on the civilian ships while the column guards, and the military boards last
Gets the most civilians out by using the column as a rearguard
A clear order of who loads and when
disadvantages: Boarding last, the column may not have the fuel or the time to board at all
Uses the military units as a sacrifice to cover the others
If the pursuit arrives early, the rearguard is trapped on the ground
options.consequence: You put the families on the ships and the soldiers between them and the pursuit. You are betting the column still has a ship left when its turn comes.

costs.resource: the column risked as rearguard for its own evacuation
costs.risk: the column guards the lift so long it cannot board itself and is left on the ground

decisionPoints.name: The Pursuit Reaches the Perimeter
decisionPoints.context: The former garrison has reached the edge of the loading point. Ships are still loading and the column is low on fuel. You can fight to hold the perimeter, start shutting the lift down early, or spend the column to buy one last ship.

options.title: Hold the perimeter, keep loading
advantages: Buys time for more ships to fill and fly
Keeps the evacuation going to the last possible moment
Keeps faith with the crowd still on the ground
disadvantages: A stand-up fight burns the column's irreplaceable fuel fast
Holding too long traps the rearguard once the ships are gone
The perimeter may break under a hard push anyway
options.consequence: You fight for every extra ship, and it costs you fuel and troops you cannot get back.

costs.resource: fuel and troops spent holding the perimeter
costs.risk: the column burns its fuel holding and cannot reach its own ships when the lift shuts down

options.title: Collapse the lift early, save the column
advantages: Gets the column boarded or clear with fuel to spare
Keeps {EMPLOYER}'s military strength intact for the rest of the war
Avoids trapping the rearguard
disadvantages: Ends the evacuation early with people still at the ramp
Leaves civilians to the turning side in order to save soldiers
A bitter trade the unit will remember
options.consequence: You save the column and close the lift early. You live with the faces still on the ground as the ramps come up.

costs.resource: the evacuation ended early
costs.risk: the people left behind are taken by the side settling scores, and the choice haunts the unit

options.title: Spend the column for a last sailing
advantages: The military units fight to the last to cover one final ship
Gets the most people out possible, including the ones the rearguard is protecting
The fullest evacuation the situation allows
disadvantages: The covering column is likely lost or left on the ground
Gives up {EMPLOYER}'s military strength to get more civilians out
Asks soldiers to be the price of one more shipload
options.consequence: You throw the column into the gap for one more ship. Most of it never gets a ramp of its own.

costs.resource: the military column spent to fill the last ship
costs.risk: the column is overrun on the ground, and the last ship is bought with the rearguard's freedom

entries.event: The evacuation begins. The loading point is held and the first ships start taking on dependents.
The crowd at the ramps grows larger than the ships can carry. The first people are turned away, and the column's fuel starts to run down.
The former garrison's pursuit is confirmed closing on the loading point, arriving sooner than hoped.
You now know how much ship space you have and how many ships arrived. The gap between who can go and who is stuck is a hard number.
The pursuit reaches the perimeter with ships still loading and the column low on fuel. The last decisions come due.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Get the ships away before the pursuit takes the loading point. Once the perimeter falls, everyone still on the ground - evacuees and rearguard alike - is left to the side the world turned to.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} pursuit drawn from the former garrison: 10-14 'Mechs of mixed weight (35-75 tons, Regular with a Veteran core that served beside {EMPLOYER} a week ago) and a fast combat-vehicle screen of hover and wheeled units racing to cut off the loading point (vehicleShare carries the screen and the mechanized pursuit). They push hard for the loading point to stop the lift and seize the highest-priority evacuees, using what they know of {EMPLOYER}'s column and habits. They fight to take the perimeter, not just to wear down the rearguard, and they break off only if holding the perimeter costs more than the people left to capture are worth.
opforSketch.behavior: An aggressive pursuit with a personal edge - former allies turned hunters, racing to close the loading point before the ships empty it. Knowing the evacuating force so well is their advantage. Their drive to reach the people on the ramps is what pushes them onto the perimeter.

forks.name: OPERATION FULL HOLDS
forks.trigger: The bulk of the available lift gets away loaded and the military column extracts within its fuel.
forks.consequence: Thousands reach safety and {EMPLOYER} keeps its column intact for the war ongoing; the evacuation becomes a hard but real success against a world that turned.

forks.name: OPERATION EVERY SOUL THAT COUNTS
forks.trigger: The high-value evacuees are all lifted and the column extracts with fuel and strength to spare.
forks.consequence: The people the turning side most wanted are denied it, and {EMPLOYER}'s column comes off whole; the clean evacuation is a morale and political win that steadies other wavering loyalists in the region.

forks.name: OPERATION LEFT ASHORE
forks.trigger: The pursuit takes the embarkation point before the lift empties, or the column runs dry and is trapped ashore.
forks.consequence: Evacuees and rearguard alike are left to the side the world turned to; {EMPLOYER} loses the people it came for and the column besides, and the cost of the last sailing is counted in those who never got one.

title: OPERATION CUT AND HOLD
skeleton: an interdiction force must sever an enemy maglev logistics spine and then defeat the rapid rail-repair-and-engineering train that will restore it within hours, so the real target is the repair capability rather than the track itself, racing to ambush the repair train where the broken line forces it to come, against escorts that know the cut will be answered fast
inspiration: the railway interdiction problem where breaking the track is easy and beating the enemy's rapid repair gangs is the real fight - rail denial on the Eastern Front, 1943-1944
situation: Breaking the enemy's railway is easy. The hard part is keeping it broken. On {WORLD}, a {TARGET_FACTION} field army in {DISTRICT} runs its heavy supply down a maglev line - the one high-capacity route that carries the ammunition, the fuel, and the replacement 'Mechs that keep its front fed. {EMPLOYER} wants that line cut, and your company drew the job. But the planners are blunt about the catch: the enemy keeps a fast rail-repair train ready. It is a self-contained crew of track-layers and bridge-builders with security to protect them, and it can put a dropped section back in service in a few hours. Cut the line and they run the repair train to the break and fix it before your damage matters. So the track is not the real target. The repair train is. Your job is to cut the line at a spot the repair train must come to - a span over rough ground, a cut with no way around it - then ambush and destroy the repair train when it arrives to work. Wreck the crew, the bridge-building gear, and the track-laying machines, and the cut stays a cut. A railway with no one to fix it is useless to the enemy. The repair train travels with an escort, and after two earlier cuts on this line, the escort knows a break will draw raiders and will be ready for an ambush. Your only read on how fast the train responds and how strong its escort is comes from how quickly they fixed those last two cuts - a pattern, not a promise.

objectives.primary: Cut the {TARGET_FACTION} maglev supply line at a point with no quick way around it, then destroy the fast repair train that comes to fix it.
objectives.secondary: Wreck the repair train's hardest-to-replace gear - the bridge-building equipment and the track-laying machines - so even a fresh crew cannot restore the line quickly.
objectives.bonus: Cut the line in a second place during the fight, so the enemy faces two breaks and one fewer repair train to fix them.

complications.name: The Cut That Mends Itself
complications.text: A dropped section on this line is back in service in hours unless the repair train is destroyed first. Wrecking the track without killing the crew that relays it is wasted effort, because the enemy fixes it before your damage matters. The break is only bait. The repair train is the prize. A cut that does not draw in and destroy the crew has done nothing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: Track damage alone is repaired on a short timer. The mission only succeeds if the repair train is destroyed. Destroying the train, not breaking the rail, is the win condition.

complications.name: Forcing the Hand
complications.text: The repair train only comes if the cut is somewhere it has to come - a span with no way around it, a stretch the enemy cannot reroute past. Cut the line where there is another route and the enemy just uses that route and never sends the train. Your ambush depends on picking a break the repair train cannot ignore.
complications.mechanicalEffect: You must cut at a point with no way around it to force the repair train to respond. Cut a spot the enemy can reroute past and the enemy simply sends its supplies another way and keeps the train out of your ambush.

complications.name: Escorts Expecting It
complications.text: The repair train travels with security. After two earlier cuts, the escort knows this line draws raiders and will be braced for an ambush at the break. The train does not roll up blind. It comes covered and alert, and your ambush has to beat an escort that is hunting for exactly what you are doing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The escort is on high alert and scouts the approach to the break before the train arrives. An ambush set in the obvious spot may be spotted and countered, so your plan must account for an escort that is actively expecting you.

decisionPoints.name: Where to Cut the Line

options.title: Drop the gorge span

costs.resource: an ambush set at the spot the enemy expects
costs.risk: the escort expects the gorge ambush and counters it before the repair train commits

options.title: Cut a remote stretch
advantages: A break far from the enemy's bases gives the ambush more time

costs.resource: a remote cut the enemy may be able to reroute past
costs.risk: the enemy reroutes around the remote break and the repair train stays home

options.title: Cut behind a chokepoint and seal it

decisionPoints.name: The Repair Train Arrives

options.title: Hit the whole train at once

The most destruction in a single blow
No second chance for the train to react

A single coordinated strike is hard to time against a moving train
Heavy resistance from an escort braced for exactly this
options.consequence: You spring on everything at once and take the whole fight together, escort and all.

costs.resource: the ambush committed against the full, alert escort
costs.risk: the braced escort blunts the strike and the repair gear survives to fix the line

Leaves the escort intact to protect a replacement crew

costs.risk: the escort catches your strike on the repair gear before it can get clear

costs.risk: the escort's sweep finds your ambush during the wait and the trap springs early, on the enemy's terms

entries.event: The maglev line is cut at the chosen point. The break is reported up the enemy's supply chain.
The enemy sends the fast repair train toward the break, with its escort scouting ahead.
The repair train nears the cut. Its escort begins scouting the approach, alert for the ambush the line has taught it to expect.
The crew starts the repair work. The repair gear is at the break and most exposed.

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Destroy the repair train before it fixes the line and withdraws. Once the crew mends the cut and pulls out intact, the line runs again and the mission has broken nothing that stays broken.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} fast repair train and its escort. The repair element is track-laying machines, bridge-building gear, and the repair crew, riding the line and appearing in the story as the prize, but destroying it is the mission. It is on high alert after the earlier cuts and is actively scouting for an ambush at the break. The escort fights to protect the crew and the line, and breaks off only if holding costs more than the repair is worth - and it rates the repair very highly.

forks.consequence: The spine is live again within hours and the operation has broken nothing that lasts; the enemy's logistics roll on, and the enemy now knows to escort this line even more heavily against the next attempt.

storyElementSeed: A lance leader lies hidden above a dropped span, watching the repair crew's lights crawl toward the break. She counts the bridge-building machines she has to destroy. The escort below is watching the same hills she is hiding in.
