A combat element braced for an ambush after two earlier cuts. It scouts the break and fights for the crew. Beating it, or slipping past it to the repair gear, is your ambush's biggest problem.

title: OPERATION SHORT TURNAROUND
skeleton: a raid force must shut down an enemy's intra-theater dropship shuttle bridge by striking its dispersal field during the brief recurring ground-turnaround windows when the shuttles are down and fuelling, racing the next lift cycle and the field's quick-reaction defense, where the shuttles are only vulnerable on the ground and the field sits among civil infrastructure that limits the methods available
inspiration: denying an enemy's air-bridge by striking the transports on the ground between sorties - the cyclic vulnerability of a shuttle lift operation
situation: The enemy is winning this campaign through the air, and the only place to stop it is on the ground, in windows of about twenty minutes at a time. On {WORLD}, the {TARGET_FACTION} command has tied its scattered holdings in {DISTRICT} together with a dropship shuttle bridge. This is a steady cycle of small dropships carrying troops, ammunition, and reaction forces between sites faster than any ground column could. It lets a spread-out enemy fight as one. {EMPLOYER} wants that bridge broken. Your company's problem is that the shuttles cannot be touched in the air. They are only exposed on the ground, in the short windows when they sit at their dispersal field to refuel and load between flights. The dispersal field is the target, and the clock is its turnaround cycle: the shuttles land, sit for a short window, and take off again. Your strike has to hit the field while they are down and cripple them before the next cycle carries them away. Miss the window and you have raided an empty airfield. The field has a quick-reaction defense built for exactly this kind of strike, and it sits among civilian buildings. It shares ground with the region's ordinary air traffic and the towns that grew up around it, which limits what methods you can use without harming the people living under the flight paths. Your read on the turnaround schedule comes from watching the cycle. It is accurate only until the enemy changes it, and a smart air commander will change it the moment he suspects the field is being watched. You have a few minutes of every cycle to break a bridge that is otherwise out of reach.

objectives.primary: Shut down the {TARGET_FACTION} shuttle bridge. Strike the dispersal field during a turnaround window and cripple or destroy the grounded shuttles before they can take off again.
objectives.secondary: Wreck the field's refueling and ground-handling gear so the bridge cannot just start up again from the same field.
objectives.bonus: Catch a reaction force while it is loading, denying the enemy both the flight and the troops it was about to move.

complications.name: Down for Twenty Minutes
complications.text: The shuttles cannot be touched in the air. They are exposed only on the ground, during the short turnaround window between flights, and that window is the whole mission. The strike has to hit the field while the shuttles are down. A strike that arrives between cycles hits an empty airfield and warns the enemy for nothing.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The shuttles can only be hit during the turnaround window on the ground. The strike must be timed to land inside that window. Arrive outside it and there are no targets, and the mission is blown.

complications.name: The Field Among the Houses
complications.text: The dispersal field shares ground with the region's civilian air traffic and the towns that ring it. Heavy or careless methods - cratering the field, firing across the approaches - will hit the people living under the flight paths. What methods you can use are limited by what they would cost the civilians, and the enemy knows it is sheltering behind them.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The civilian buildings around the field limit which methods you can use. Careless fire or wide-area destruction causes civilian casualties and a reputation penalty, forcing the strike into slower, more precise methods.

complications.name: The Schedule That Moves
complications.text: Your read of the turnaround cycle only holds as long as the enemy keeps it. An air commander who suspects his field is being watched will change the timing, shift the windows, or send the shuttles to other fields. The schedule you planned around may no longer exist at the moment you commit.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The turnaround schedule grows less reliable if the enemy notices he is being watched. A changed cycle can leave the strike arriving at the wrong window, forcing an abort or an improvised attack on a field where the shuttles are already scattering.

decisionPoints.name: How to Hit the Field
decisionPoints.context: The shuttles are down for only a few minutes, and the field sits among civilians. How you strike decides what you can destroy and what it costs.

options.title: Fast precise strike on the grounded shuttles

Precise fire spares the surrounding towns
Destroys the bridge's actual carrying capacity
disadvantages: A precise strike is slower to deliver inside a short window
You have to get close to a defended field
Few shuttles destroyed if the window is tight
options.consequence: You go for the shuttles cleanly and accept that being precise inside a narrow window limits how many you get.

costs.resource: fewer shuttles destroyed, in exchange for precision and no civilian harm
costs.risk: the window closes before enough shuttles are crippled and the bridge survives

options.title: Wreck the fuelling and handling instead
advantages: Wrecking the ground gear grounds the bridge even if the shuttles escape
The refueling and handling gear is fixed and easier to hit than moving shuttles
Denies the field as a base, not just one cycle's flights
disadvantages: The shuttles themselves may take off and operate from somewhere else
Fuel fires near civilian buildings risk the towns
An intact shuttle fleet just moves to another field and keeps flying
options.consequence: You break the field's ability to turn shuttles around and let the shuttles flee. You are betting a bridge with no field is a broken bridge.

costs.resource: the shuttles allowed to escape if they can take off
costs.risk: the shuttles move to another field and the bridge starts up again from there

options.title: Seize the field, hold the window open
advantages: Taking the field lets you destroy the shuttles and the ground gear at your own pace
Also catches whatever lands in the next cycle
The most complete shutdown, if you can hold it
disadvantages: Holding the field brings the full quick-reaction defense and more
Holding a field among civilians means fighting in their streets
The longer you hold, the heavier the enemy's response
options.consequence: You take the field outright and turn its own turnaround clock into a trap. You are betting you can hold it long enough to matter.

costs.resource: the whole company committed to holding contested ground
costs.risk: the quick-reaction defense and follow-on forces pin the company on the field

decisionPoints.name: The Window Is Wrong
decisionPoints.context: You commit and find the enemy has changed the cycle. The field is half-empty, fewer shuttles are down than expected, and the defense is already stirring. You can press the strike anyway, abort and try the next cycle, or switch to wrecking what is there.

options.title: Press the strike anyway
advantages: Hits whatever shuttles are down before the chance is gone
Keeps the initiative instead of handing it to a changed schedule
Some damage now beats a perfect strike that never comes
disadvantages: A half-empty field offers fewer targets
The stirring defense meets the strike more ready than planned
Commits to a weaker attack on the enemy's changed terms
options.consequence: You take what the changed cycle left on the field and accept a partial strike against a defense that is more ready.

costs.resource: a weaker strike on the enemy's terms
costs.risk: the thin target and the alert defense turn the strike into a costly half-result

options.title: Abort and wait for the next cycle
advantages: Keeps the force intact for a full strike when the windows line up again
Avoids a weak attack on bad terms
A patient strike on a proper window does more damage
disadvantages: The enemy, now alerted, may change the schedule again or harden the field
Waiting lets the bridge run more flights in the meantime
The next good window may not come before your time runs out
options.consequence: You pull back for a better cycle. You are betting the enemy gives you one before your chance or your contract runs out.

costs.resource: flights let through while you wait for a clean window
costs.risk: the alerted enemy hardens the field or moves it and no clean window ever comes

options.title: Shift to wrecking the field's infrastructure
advantages: Turns a bad shuttle-window into a strike on the fixed ground gear
Denies the field no matter how many shuttles are down
Salvages a result from a changed schedule
disadvantages: Gives up the chance to catch the shuttles themselves
Damaging the ground gear near civilians still carries a cost
The untouched shuttles just keep flying from somewhere else
options.consequence: You give up on the shuttles you cannot catch and break the field they fly from, taking the shutdown you can still get.

costs.resource: the shuttles given up in order to hit the field
costs.risk: the bridge starts up again from another field and the strike on the ground gear only delays it

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Cripple the shuttles and the field within the turnaround window, before the next cycle carries them out of reach. Once the shuttles are airborne again, the bridge is intact and the strike has hit empty ground.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} dispersal field's defense: a quick-reaction element of 6-9 'Mechs (30-65 tons, Regular with a Veteran lead) held ready to protect the field against exactly this kind of strike, plus a combat-vehicle slice of mobile air-defense and security units around the field (vehicleShare carries the air-defense and ground-security vehicles). The shuttles themselves and the ground crews appear in the story as the targets. The defense responds within minutes of a strike and fights to cover the shuttles until they can take off. It does not chase far beyond the field, since its job is to hold the ground long enough for the bridge to escape.
opforSketch.behavior: A field defense built around the turnaround clock: hold the field, cover the grounded shuttles, and buy the minutes they need to take off. It reacts fast and fights hard up close, counting on the strike's narrow window and the civilians around the field to limit the attacker's options.

forks.consequence: The bridge endures and the enemy, now alerted, moves or hardens the field; the shuttles keep its scattered holdings stitched together, and the next strike faces a wary, defended target.

storyElementSeed: A strike leader watches a dispersal field through the dawn haze. She counts the squat shapes of shuttles on the field and the houses just past the perimeter fence. She has the length of one turnaround to do this, and not a minute to waste on the wrong target.

title: OPERATION HARD CURRENCY
skeleton: a raid force must intercept an enemy field-army's hard-currency payroll and war-chest convoy to break the mercenary contracts its pay sustains, where capturing the chest intact funds friendly operations and merely destroying it only denies, and the convoy hides among civilian armored transit, so the crux is taking the money whole rather than wrecking it, exploiting the era's split-loyalty mercenary economy
inspiration: the strategic raid to seize an enemy's war-chest and unpaid-mercenary vulnerability - the pay-chest interdiction of a mercenary-dependent army
situation: An army that fights with hired soldiers lives or dies by its payroll, and the {TARGET_FACTION} field army in {DISTRICT} is about to move a whole season's pay down one road. The war on {WORLD} has drawn mercenaries to both sides, and much of the enemy's line is held by hired battalions whose contracts are plain: no pay, no fight. {EMPLOYER} has learned that the enemy's hard-currency war-chest - the coin and certified notes that fund those payrolls - is being moved up to a paymaster's depot to settle the season's contracts. {EMPLOYER} wants it taken. Not destroyed - taken. Capturing the chest does two things at once. It cuts off the pay that keeps the enemy's mercenaries in the line, and it funds {EMPLOYER}'s own operations and contracts in a war where everyone is short of money. Destroying the chest only does the first, and it burns money both sides need. So your company's job is a raid that ends with the money in your hands and undamaged: intercept the convoy, take the chest whole, and carry it off before the escort or a reaction force can get it back. The convoy will not stand out. Hard currency travels disguised, hidden inside ordinary civilian armored transit - bullion vans, secure freight, the armored cars that move payrolls and valuables on any world. Picking the real chest out of the decoys and the civilian traffic is half the problem. Your only tip on which vehicle carries the chest and when it moves comes from a paymaster's clerk. It is two days old, and it is worth exactly as much as the clerk is honest.

objectives.primary: Intercept the {TARGET_FACTION} war-chest convoy and capture the hard-currency chest undamaged, before the escort or a reaction force can get it back.
objectives.secondary: Pick out the real chest from the decoy and civilian armored vehicles without wrecking the wrong one or harming civilians.
objectives.bonus: Take the paymaster and the contract records along with the chest, revealing which enemy mercenary units are owed what - and which might be bought off.

complications.name: Whole, Not Wrecked
complications.text: Hard currency burns. A destroyed chest cuts off the enemy's mercenaries' pay, but it funds no one and leaves a war that is already short of money even poorer. The raid only fully succeeds if the money is taken undamaged. That rules out the easy methods: no shelling the convoy, and no torching the armored car that might be carrying the chest.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The war-chest must be captured undamaged. Attacks strong enough to cripple a normal convoy risk destroying the currency, so you have to disable and seize the carrying vehicle without wrecking it.

complications.name: Money in Plain Wrapping
complications.text: The chest does not ride in anything marked. It moves inside ordinary civilian armored transit - bullion vans, secure freight, payroll cars - mixed in with decoys and the real civilian traffic of a working district. Picking the true vehicle out from the fakes and the innocent ones is the difference between a clean capture and a wrecked decoy while the real money drives on past.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The war-chest is hidden among decoy and civilian armored vehicles. Hit the wrong one and the real chest slips past. Hit a civilian one and you take a reputation and contract penalty.

complications.name: The Clerk's Honesty
complications.text: Your whole plan rests on a two-day-old tip from a paymaster's clerk: which van, which route, which hour. A clerk leaks for money, out of spite, or because he was ordered to. If the tip is bait, it sends your raid onto a decoy or into an ambush while the real chest takes another road. This tip is the whole plan, and you cannot check whether it is true until you are already committed.
complications.mechanicalEffect: The leaked convoy details may not be reliable. If the tip is false or planted, the raid hits a decoy or a waiting counter-ambush while the real chest moves untouched on a different route.

decisionPoints.name: How to Take the Convoy
decisionPoints.context: The chest has to come out undamaged, and you have to find the real vehicle among decoys and civilians. How you hit the convoy decides whether you get the money or just a wreck.

costs.resource: time spent searching a stopped convoy
costs.risk: the reaction force arrives while you are still sorting the convoy and takes the chest back

options.title: Strike the identified conveyance only

Keeps your exposure and civilian entanglement low
A quick capture if the tip is right
disadvantages: Bets everything on the tip being accurate
Hit the wrong vehicle and you get a wrecked decoy and a lost chance
If the real chest is elsewhere, it drives on while you hit the decoy
options.consequence: You trust the clerk and strike the one van. You are betting the tip named the real money.

costs.resource: the whole raid staked on the tip being accurate
costs.risk: the named vehicle is a decoy and the real chest escapes on another road

advantages: Following the convoy shows which vehicle is handled like the real chest

disadvantages: If the convoy spots the tail, it scatters or races to safety

reactionTimeline.hardDeadline: Take the chest undamaged and break contact before the reaction force arrives and gets it back. Once it does, the money is back in enemy hands and the raid was spent for nothing, or worse, it burned money both sides needed.

opforSketch.composition: A {TARGET_FACTION} convoy escort plus a reaction force. The escort is a combat element of 5-8 'Mechs (30-60 tons, Regular with a Veteran lead) and a fast combat-vehicle screen riding with the convoy among the armored vehicles (vehicleShare carries the screen and the convoy's own armored vehicles). The reaction force is a reinforced lance to a company of 6-10 medium and heavy 'Mechs (45-75 tons, Regular), sent the moment the convoy is hit. The paymaster, the clerks, and the real civilian drivers appear in the story. The escort fights to protect the chest and to buy the reaction force time, and it will not abandon the money while it can still fight for it.
opforSketch.behavior: An escort guarding something it knows is priceless. It fights to keep the chest moving, or to destroy it rather than let the raiders have it, until help arrives. It values the money above its own survival, up to a point, and the reaction force drives hard to recover money the enemy's whole line depends on.

forks.name: OPERATION FULL CHEST
forks.trigger: The hard-currency war-chest is captured intact and carried off before the reaction force recovers it.
forks.consequence: The enemy's mercenaries go unpaid and begin to waver in the line, while {EMPLOYER}'s own coffers and contracts are funded; the captured coin shifts the war's economy in {EMPLOYER}'s favor.

forks.name: OPERATION OPEN LEDGER
forks.trigger: The chest, the paymaster, and the contract ledgers are all taken intact.
forks.consequence: {EMPLOYER} learns exactly which enemy mercenary units are owed what and which are ripe to be bought; the war-chest funds a counter-recruiting campaign that peels hired battalions off the enemy's line.

forks.name: OPERATION BAD PAPER
forks.trigger: The leak was false and the raid hits a decoy, or the reaction force recovers the chest, or the currency is destroyed in the taking.
forks.consequence: Either the enemy's payroll reaches its mercenaries and the line holds, or the coin burns and both sides are the poorer; the raid is spent, and a blown attempt teaches the enemy to guard its war-chest harder.

storyElementSeed: A raid leader looks down a line of disabled armored vans. One of them holds a season's pay for a battalion of hired soldiers. A paymaster's clerk swears he knows which one - for a price - while the reaction force's dust rises on the horizon.

assetDetails.detail: A season's pay for the enemy's hired battalions. Captured, it funds {EMPLOYER} and breaks the enemy's line. Destroyed, it only leaves everyone poorer. The whole raid turns on taking it undamaged.
The paymaster's clerk who tipped off the convoy. He is your only lead on which van carries the chest, and his tip may be honest, mistaken, or planted to steer the raid onto a decoy.
